result_semantic_payload.summary: All four USDT transfers visible in the captured logs are attributed to the account name 'chenwei' in /logs/app1.log; no transfer events appear in /logs/app2.log, and no other user performs a transfer. However, the evidence does NOT support treating 'chenwei' in the two systems as the same person. /README.txt states the two systems are unrelated internal systems that share no account database, and the two 'chenwei' instances are only linked by an identical username string — no shared identifier (no SID, no email, no full name, no auth token, no shared account DB, no overlapping IP space: app2 uses 10.20.0.x private addresses, app1 uses 203.0.113.77 / 198.51.100.23 public addresses). The README additionally asserts that 'chenwei' is a finance-department employee on an office workstation, which is contextual metadata rather than proven identity binding. This is the classic same-name-account trap: name collision across independent systems is not identity equivalence.

claim_candidates.text: Every USDT transfer recorded in the captured logs is attributed to the account name 'chenwei' in /logs/app1.log: 2024-03-01 09:15:03 amount=30000USDT dest=TBait8888Wallet, and 2024-03-02 22:43:55 amount=12000USDT dest=TBait8888Wallet. Total visible transfer volume is 42000 USDT to a single destination string.

Both chenwei transfers in app1.log occur within roughly two minutes of a successful LOGIN for user=chenwei from the same log stream (09:14:22 LOGIN ip=203.0.113.77 -> 09:15:03 TRANSFER -> 09:16:44 LOGOUT on 2024-03-01; 22:41:10 LOGIN ip=198.51.100.23 -> 22:43:55 TRANSFER on 2024-03-02), so the transfers are consistent with the chenwei session in that system, but the log itself does not record auth
limitations: The log format provides no session id, so LOGIN-to-TRANSFER linkage is temporal co-occurrence only.
The log is a plain text file with no integrity protection (md5 empty in metadata), so attribution is only as trustworthy as the log source.
